This causes some difficulty, however, when trying to define a tensor product functor:

\bigotimes:\underbrace{\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}\times\cdots\times\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}}_{D\text{ times}}\to\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}\,,

since using the Segre outer product leads to this functor not automatically being defined for all
D
-tuples of finite-dimensional real vector spaces (in contrast to the situation where the “one arbitrary choice for all vector spaces” approach had been utilized instead), since the Segre outer product only defines the functor for those
D
-tuples which consist exclusively of
\mathbb{R}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}
’s.

So the concern which needs to be addressed is the following: will different arbitrary choices of vector space satisfying the universal property of the tensor product to use as the value of the tensor product functor for all remaining
D
-tuples lead to (meaningfully) different tensor product functors? Will the study of one type of tensor product functor defined partially in terms of the Segre outer product lead to different conclusions compared to the tensor product functor defined on objects by always using the aforementioned quotient space construction?

First an interlude which will soon prove to be relevant. In order to define a tensor product functor, it actually suffices to define it only on objects, doing so by choosing for each
D
-tuple of finite-dimensional real vector spaces an element of the equivalence class of vector spaces satisfying the universal property for them. This is because the universal property can then be used to automatically define the tensor product functor on morphisms.

More concretely, for linear functions
\mathbb{V}_{1}\xrightarrow{f_{1}}\mathbb{W}_{1}
, …,
\mathbb{V}_{D}\xrightarrow{f_{D}}\mathbb{W}_{D}
, what one wants to do is have a choice of linear function from the chosen value
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{V}_{d}
of the tensor product functor for
\mathbb{V}_{1},\dots,\mathbb{V}_{D}
to the chosen value
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{W}_{d}
of the tensor product functor for
\mathbb{W}_{1},\dots,\mathbb{W}_{D}
, so that the chosen linear function can then represent the chosen value
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}f_{d}
for the tensor product functor on the morphisms
f_{1},\dots,f_{D}
. The universal property automatically makes such a choice.

Consider the Cartesian product of linear functions (which itself is linear):

\mathbb{V}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{V}_{D}\xrightarrow{f_{1}\times\cdots\times f_{D}}\mathbb{W}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{W}_{D}\,,

given via the rule of assignment
(f_{1}\times\cdots\times f_{D})(\mathbf{v}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{v}_{D})=(f_{1}(\mathbf{v}_{1}),\dots,f_{D}(\mathbf{v}_{D}))
. Then

\bigotimes_{\mathbb{W}}\circ(f_{1}\times\cdots\times f_{D}):\mathbb{V}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{V}_{D}\to\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{W}_{d}

is multilinear (since the function
\bigotimes_{\mathbb{W}}:\mathbb{W}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{W}_{D}\to\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{W}_{d}
is multilinear). Therefore the universal property of the tensor product for
(\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{V}_{d},\bigotimes_{\mathbb{V}})
guarantees the existence of a
unique
linear function
h:\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{V}_{d}\to\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{W}_{d}
such that
h\circ\bigotimes_{\mathbb{V}}=\bigotimes_{\mathbb{W}}\circ(f_{1}\times\cdots\times f_{D})
.

It turns out that, given the choices of
(\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{V}_{d},\bigotimes_{\mathbb{V}})
for the value of the tensor product functor on
\mathbb{V}_{1}
, …,
\mathbb{V}_{D}
, and
(\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{W}_{d},\bigotimes_{\mathbb{W}})
for the value of the tensor product functor on
\mathbb{W}_{1}
, …,
\mathbb{W}_{D}
, then the linear function
h:\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{V}_{d}\to\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{W}_{d}
defined uniquely via the universal property of the tensor product is the natural choice for the value of the tensor product functor on
f_{1},\dots,f_{D}
, i.e. the natural choice is given by defining
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}f_{d}\overset{\text{def}}{=}h
.

The choice is natural in the following sense: given one tensor product functor
\bigotimes^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}}
defined on objects by making one class of arbitrary choices of vector spaces satisfying the universal property, and defined on morphisms by using the arbitrary choices on objects and the universal property in the manner explained above, and another tensor product functor
\bigotimes^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}}
defined on objects by making another class of arbitrary choices of vector spaces satisfying the universal property, and also defined on morphisms by using the universal property as explained above to extend the arbitrary choices on objects, then the two functors
\bigotimes^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}}
and
\bigotimes^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}}
will always be naturally isomorphic
121
121

121

“Natural isomorphism” is a precisely defined notion of category theory, cf. footnote
108
of appendix
A.7
.
, or in other words they will be for all intents and purposes entirely equivalent. This is because of the unique isomorphisms which, due to the universal property, exist between the arbitrary choices made on objects by the first functor and the arbitrary choices made on objects by the second functor, and because both functors were defined on morphisms by using the unique linear functions found using the universal property in the way which was described above.

Note that the tensor product of linear transformations as it has been defined in section
6.2
is the same definition one gets by using the Segre outer product to define the tensor product functor on
\mathbb{R}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}
’s and then using the universal property to define the values of the tensor product functor on morphisms. So even though the tensor product functor as defined in this review is slightly different, at least on
\mathbb{R}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}
’s and linear functions between them, then the tensor product functor more commonly defined elsewhere, both functors are still naturally isomorphic to one another, and this remains true regardless of which arbitrary choices of vector spaces satisfying the universal property are used to define the tensor product functor on
D
-tuples of vector spaces for which not all of the
\mathbb{V}_{d}
’s are equal to
\mathbb{R}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}
for some
[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]
. Therefore, for the sake of simplicity, when at least one of the vector spaces
\mathbb{V}_{d}
is not equal to some
\mathbb{R}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}
, for this review define the
D
-fold tensor product of those vector spaces (and associated
D
-linear map) via the usual construction as found e.g. in chapter 2 of
[
14
]
. Moreover, for this review the value of the tensor product functor on morphisms will always use the linear maps generated by the universal product as described above.

A.10.2
Objects of the Category of Finite-Dimensional Real
D
-Factorized

Tensor Spaces

For a given
D\geq 1
, the objects of
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{D}
consist of three data:

(i)

a finite-dimensional real vector space
\mathbb{T}
,

(ii)

a
D
-tuple of finite-dimensional real vectors spaces
(\mathbb{V}_{1},\dots,\mathbb{V}_{D})
,

(iii)

a multilinear map

\bigotimes:\mathbb{V}_{1}\times\mathbb{V}_{2}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{V}_{D}\to\mathbb{T}

which satisfies the universal property of the tensor product.

The standard example will always be (where
{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{577006}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{577006}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{505259}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{505254}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]\overset{\text{def}}{=}\bigtimes_{d=1}^{D}[M_{d}]}
) the special case when

\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{627204}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{627204}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{453877}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{453878}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}
,
\mathbb{V}_{1}=\mathbb{R}^{[M_{1}]}
,
\mathbb{V}_{2}=\mathbb{R}^{[M_{2}]}
, …,
\mathbb{V}_{D}=\mathbb{R}^{[M_{D}]}
, and
\bigotimes
denotes the Segre outer product.

A.10.3
Morphisms of the Category of Finite-Dimensional Real
D
-Factorized Tensor Spaces

Given two objects
\mathbb{V}
and
\mathbb{W}
of
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{D}
, a morphism
\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{W}
is any linear function of the form:

\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}f_{d}:\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{W}\,,\quad\quad f_{1}:\mathbb{V}_{1}\to\mathbb{W}_{1}\,,\dots\,,f_{d}:\mathbb{V}_{d}\to\mathbb{W}_{d}\,,\dots\,,f_{D}:\mathbb{V}_{D}\to\mathbb{W}_{D}\,.

Here
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}f_{d}
refers to the unique linear function
\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{W}
such that

\left(\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}f_{d}\right)\circ\bigotimes_{\mathbb{V}}=\bigotimes_{\mathbb{W}}\circ(f_{1}\times\cdots\times f_{D})

which exists since both
\mathbb{V}
and
\mathbb{W}
satisfy the universal property of the
D
-fold tensor product, cf. the discussion section
A.10.1
above. It can be thought of as the unique linear function
\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{W}
corresponding to the multilinear function
\bigotimes_{\mathbb{W}}\circ(f_{1}\times\cdots\times f_{D})
which is compatible with the tensor product structure on
\mathbb{V}
(which is encapsulated via
\bigotimes_{\mathbb{V}}
).

In this review the standard example will always be functions of the form:

\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}f_{d}:\mathbb{R}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{627204}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{627204}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{453877}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{453878}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}\to\mathbb{R}^{[N_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{627204}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{627204}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{453877}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{453878}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}\,,\quad\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}f_{d}:\mathbf{v}_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathbf{v}_{D}\mapsto f_{1}(\mathbf{v}_{1})\otimes\cdots\otimes f_{D}(\mathbf{v}_{D})\,,

where it suffices to define the function only for elementary tensors due to the universal property of the tensor product, and where
\otimes
refers to the Segre outer product; compare this with section
6.2
.

Tensor spaces
\mathbb{V}
,
\mathbb{W}
are
isomorphic
(as
D
-factorized tensor spaces) if there are morphisms in
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{D}
:

f:\mathbb{V}\to\mathbb{W}\,,\quad g:\mathbb{W}\to\mathbb{V}\,,

such that
g\circ f=\operatorname{Id}_{\mathbb{V}}
and
f\circ g=\operatorname{Id}_{\mathbb{W}}
.

A.10.4
Remarks about the Category of Finite-Dimensional Real
D
-Factorized Tensor Spaces

Analogous to
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}
and
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}_{1}
, both the objects and morphisms of
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{1}
and
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}
are essentially the same, making both categories for all intents and purposes essentially the same. Thus, from now
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{1}
will be redefined so that
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{1}=\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}
.

Also analogous to the multi-index categories, for any
O>D
one also always has
\binom{O-1}{D-1}
distinct forgetful functors from
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{O}
to
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{D}
, with each distinct forgetful functor corresponding to a different contiguous partition of the
O
vector spaces
\mathbb{V}_{1},\dots,\mathbb{V}_{O}
.

As an example, consider the case when
O=3
,
D=2
,
\mathbb{V}=\mathbb{R}^{[24]\times[24]}
,
\bigotimes_{\mathbb{V}}=\otimes_{\operatorname{Kr}}
(the Kronecker matrix product),
\mathbb{V}_{1}=\mathbb{R}^{[4]\times[2]}
,
\mathbb{V}_{2}=\mathbb{R}^{[3]\times[3]}
, and
\mathbb{V}_{3}=\mathbb{R}^{[2]\times[4]}
. Then
\mathscr{F}_{12|3}(\mathbb{V})
corresponds to
\mathbb{V}_{1}=\mathbb{R}^{[12]\times[6]}
and
\mathbb{V}_{2}=\mathbb{R}^{[2]\times[4]}
, while
\mathscr{F}_{1|23}(\mathbb{V})
corresponds to
\mathbb{V}_{1}=\mathbb{R}^{[4]\times[2]}
and
\mathbb{V}_{2}=\mathbb{R}^{[6]\times[12]}
.

Also, as before, any morphism in
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{O}
between
\mathbb{V}
and
\mathbb{W}
will also be a morphism in
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{D}
between
\mathscr{F}_{Q}(\mathbb{V})
and
\mathscr{F}_{Q}(\mathbb{W})
for any contiguous partition
Q
of
[O]
into
D
blocks, but there will also always be morphisms between
\mathscr{F}_{Q}(\mathbb{V})
and
\mathscr{F}_{Q}(\mathbb{W})
in
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{D}
which are not morphisms in
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{O}
. Preserving
O
-fold tensor product structure is sufficient to preserve any coarser
D
-fold tensor product structure, but preserving
D
-fold tensor product structure is
not
enough to guarantee also preserving
O
-fold tensor product structure for
O>D
.

Note that, for each
D\geq 1
, at least as long as the
D
-fold tensor product functor is defined in any of the naturally isomorphic ways described above in section
A.10.1
, the category
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{D}
is equivalent to the image of the
D
-fold tensor product functor:

\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}:\underbrace{\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}\times\cdots\times\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}}_{D\text{ times}}\to\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}\,,

in the sense that every object of
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{D}
is isomorphic as a
D
-factorized tensor space (isomorphic in
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{D}
) to an object
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}\mathbb{V}_{d}
in the image of the
D
-fold tensor product functor
\bigotimes_{d=1}^{D}
.

Note also that, by choosing coordinates, every object of
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{D}
is isomorphic as a
D
-factorized tensor space to
\mathbb{R}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{627204}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{627204}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{453877}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{453878}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}
for some multi-index set
[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{577006}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{577006}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{505259}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{505254}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]
of order
D
. More specifically, given an object
\mathbb{T}
of
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Tens}_{D}
which has the
D
-tuple of vector spaces
(\mathbb{V}_{1},\dots,\mathbb{V}_{D})
as its “tensor factors”, and if
M_{d}\overset{\text{def}}{=}\dim(\mathbb{V}_{d})
for all
d\in[D]
, then the aforementioned
[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{577006}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{577006}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{505259}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{505254}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]
equals
\bigtimes_{d=1}^{D}[M_{d}]
. One construction of such an isomorphism is described in appendix
A.6.2
.

Thus, even when considering
D
-factorized tensor spaces and
D
-fold tensor product structure, there is still is no loss of generality in restricting attention only to coordinate spaces
\mathbb{R}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{627204}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{627204}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{453877}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{453878}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[D]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}
with the Segre outer product as their tensor product, analogous to the situation for vector spaces.

Appendix A.11
Tensor Shape Functors

The following sections describe the interpretation of the dual tensor shape functor as well as how to relate general linear functions to those in the image of
\mathfrak{F}
.

A.11.1
Interpretation of Dual Tensor Shape Functor

By construction, the tensor shape functor
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}\to\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}
can be considered the restriction of a free functor
\mathfrak{F}:\mathsf{Fin}\mathsf{Set}\to\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}
, since
\mathfrak{F}([M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}])=\mathbb{R}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}
satisfies the universal property of the free real vector space generated by
[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]
, cf. endnote
of section
4
or section 3.1.2 of
[
129
]
.

Any functor has a corresponding opposite functor which behaves the same on objects and morphisms as the original functor. The tensor shape functor in particular has an opposite functor:

\mathfrak{F}^{\operatorname{op}}:\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}^{\operatorname{op}}\,.

The universal property of the free real vector space implies that, for any finite-dimensional real vector space
\mathbb{V}
, the following functors
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}
are naturally equivalent:

\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}}(\mathfrak{F}^{op}(\cdot),\mathbb{V})\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Set}}(\cdot,\mathscr{F}(\mathbb{V}))=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Set}}(\cdot,\mathbb{V})\,,

where
\mathscr{F}
denotes the forgetful functor
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}\to\mathsf{Set}
. Note that
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Set}}([M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}],\mathbb{V})\overset{\text{def}}{=}\mathbb{V}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}
is a finite-dimensional vector space (for any multi-index set
[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]
and finite-dimensional real vector space
\mathbb{V}
, where addition and scalar multiplication are defined “pointwise” for the functions, and the dimension as a real vector space is equal to the product of the cardinality of
[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]
and the dimension of
\mathbb{V}
as a real vector space, i.e.
\dim(\mathbb{V}^{[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]})=|[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]|\dim(\mathbb{V})
).

When
\mathbb{V}=\mathbb{R}
, this gives the following natural equivalence of functors
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}
:

\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}}(\mathfrak{F}^{op}(\cdot),\mathbb{R})\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Set}}(\cdot,\mathbb{R})\,.

By definition, the dual tensor shape functor
\mathfrak{F}^{\ast}:\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}^{\operatorname{op}}\to\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}
is the same as the functor in the right-hand side of the natural equivalence written above:

\mathfrak{F}^{\ast}\overset{\text{def}}{=}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Set}}(\cdot,\mathbb{R})\,,

so the above equivalence of functors also implies the following:

\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}}(\mathfrak{F}^{op}(\cdot),\mathbb{R})\cong\mathfrak{F}^{\ast}\,.

Similarly, definitionally for the dual functor
\mathfrak{D}:\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}^{op}\to\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}
one has that:

\mathfrak{D}\overset{\text{def}}{=}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}}(\cdot,\mathbb{R})\,.

Therefore one can rewrite left-hand side of the above natural equivalence:

\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}}(\mathfrak{F}^{op}(\cdot),\mathbb{R})=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}}(\cdot,\mathbb{R})\circ\mathfrak{F}^{\operatorname{op}}=\mathfrak{D}\circ\mathfrak{F}^{\operatorname{op}}\,.

Combing the above, the universal property of the free vector space finally leds to the equivalence:

\mathfrak{D}\circ\mathfrak{F}^{\operatorname{op}}\cong\mathfrak{F}^{\ast}\,,

i.e. the dual tensor shape functor
\mathfrak{F}^{\ast}
is a naturally equivalent functor to the functor resulting from composing the opposite functor
\mathfrak{F}^{\operatorname{op}}
of the tensor shape functor
\mathfrak{F}
with the dual functor
\mathfrak{D}
. This is the justification for the name “dual tensor shape functor” and also explains why
\mathfrak{F}^{\ast}(f)
always corresponds to the adjoint linear transformation of
\mathfrak{F}(f)
for any morphism
f
in
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}
.

A.11.2
Combinatorial Linear Algebra

The sub-category of
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}
which is the image
122
122

122

That the image of a functor in this case is a bona fide subcategory, i.e. closed under composition of morphisms, can be derived as a corollary of the fact that the functor is injective on objects.

of the tensor shape functor
\mathfrak{F}
can be thought of as a subset of (multi)linear algebra which is secretly entirely combinatorial in nature, in the sense that all problems can be reduced to problems about multi-index sets and functions between them via the tensor shape functor. Such problems include (but are not limited to) permuting modes of a tensor and reshaping a tensor. The objects of this category are all of the coordinate spaces, and the morphisms are a heavily restricted subset of the possible linear functions between them, namely linear functions of the form
\mathfrak{F}(f)
for some function between multi-index sets
f
.

However, it is possible to use this very limited subset of linear functions to recover all non-zero linear functions
123
123

123

Which is the same thing as all linear functions with rank greater than or equal to one.
by combining them with changes of basis

124

124

In more algebraic terms: linear automorphisms, or linear self-isomorphisms, of vector spaces.
of the coordinate spaces. Specifically,

. If the rank is at least one, then a trick can be employed to make everything work when the null space of

However, the fact that the zero linear map can not factorize this way, and that an ugly trick is required whenever the null space is non-zero, correctly suggests that
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}
is not the “correct” category to which one should attempt to reduce all multilinear algebra. The problem is that
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}
does not have any “zero object” and consequently no notions of “zero morphisms” or “sending an element to zero”, whereas
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}
does. Thus these aspects of
\mathsf{Fin}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{Vect}
cannot be completely or directly captured using
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}
and the tensor shape functor
\mathfrak{F}
, even after changing basises.

This can be fairly easily rectified however by replacing
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}
with the category of
pointed
multi-index sets
125
125

125

The idea is analogous to the “four subspace” diagrams of Gilbert Strang (when the multi-index sets are index sets).

\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}^{\star}
, i.e. multi-index sets with an extra “point”/element
\star
appended to represent a notion of “zero object”, and functions
f:[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{704563}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O_{1}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{704563}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O_{1}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{646335}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O_{1}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.63889pt}{\resizebox{712089}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.05pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O_{1}]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]\to[N_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{704563}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O_{2}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{704563}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O_{2}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{646335}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O_{2}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.63889pt}{\resizebox{712089}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.05pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O_{2}]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]
limited to those which send the zero points
\star_{M}
of their domains to the zero points
\star_{N}
of their codomains. This requires modifying the Cartesian product operation to be the so-called “smash product” which ensures that the product of pointed multi-index sets is still a pointed multi-index sets (i.e. only has
one
zero point, not multiple), and some other relatively straightforward changes. In particular, the category
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}
can be “embedded” as a subcategory of
\bm{\mathsf{MltIdx}}^{\star}
in a fairly obvious way, so there is no “loss of information”. The details of these constructions are tedious and outside the scope of this review.

A.11.3
Non-Zero Null Space Trick

As explained in endnote
A.14
, without loss of generality one may assume that the multi-index sets
[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{704563}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O_{1}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{704563}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O_{1}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{646335}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O_{1}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.63889pt}{\resizebox{712089}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.05pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O_{1}]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]
and
[N_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{704563}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O_{2}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{704563}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O_{2}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{646335}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O_{2}]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.63889pt}{\resizebox{712089}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.05pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O_{2}]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]
are index sets
[M]
and
[N]
respectively. Then one possibly way of choosing
\mathscr{B}_{S}
and
\mathscr{B}_{T}
consists of making the right singular vectors the elements of
\mathscr{B}_{S}
and

\tau_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}\quad\text{where }\mathbf{u}_{i}\text{ is a left singular vector and }\quad\tau_{i}=\begin{cases}\sigma_{i}&\sigma_{i}>0\\
1&\sigma_{i}=0\end{cases}

(
\sigma_{i}
denote singular values) the first elements of
\mathscr{B}_{T}
, with
\mathscr{B}_{T}
itself being an arbitrary completion of the
\tau_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}
to a basis of
\mathbb{R}^{N}
. Then clearly
\mathcal{L}
sends every element of
\mathscr{B}_{S}
either to an element of
\mathscr{B}_{T}
(when the corresponding
\sigma_{i}
is non-zero) or to
\mathbf{0}
.

Starting from this, the first attempt at choosing
\mathscr{A}_{S}
sends the elements of
\mathscr{B}_{S}
to the standard basis of
\mathbb{R}^{M}
, and the first attempt at choosing
\mathscr{A}_{T}
sends the elements of
\mathscr{B}_{T}
to the standard basis of
\mathbb{R}^{M}
.

This works without any problems in the case that
\mathcal{L}
is injective (i.e. all of the singular values are non-zero, or equivalently the null space is zero), since in this case
\mathscr{C}
can be chosen to be
\mathfrak{F}(f)
for
f:[M]\to[N]
which embeds
[M]
into
[N]
. (Note that
\mathcal{L}:\mathbb{R}^{M}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}
being injective necessarily implies that
M<N
.) However
\mathscr{A}_{S}
must be modified when
\mathcal{L}
is not injective.

The idea of the trick is that “sending
k
dimensions to zero” is the same as “sending
k+1
dimensions to the same (one) dimension”, and thus requires the assumption that there is at least one dimension in the image of
\mathcal{L}
, i.e. that
\mathcal{L}
has rank of at least one.

Assume without loss of generality that
\mathscr{A}_{S}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}}
sends a right singular vector corresponding to a non-zero singular value to the first standard basis vector, and that
\mathscr{A}_{S}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}}
sends all of the right singular vectors corresponding to zero singular values to the
2
nd through
(k+1)
’st standard basis vectors. (If there are any remaining right singular vectors corresponding to non-zero singular values,

Appendix A.12
Non-Commutative Polynomials

Informally speaking, the equivalence between tensors and non-commutative polynomials can be understood by applying the following rules.

Rule 1:
Only tensors of the exact same shape can be added. All other addition is formal addition.

(One way the notion of formal addition can be made rigorous is by taking the direct sum of vector spaces, in this case all of the
\mathbb{R}^{[I_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}
for all possible shapes
[I_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]
. Compare with e.g.
[
294
]
.)

Example of non-formal addition:

\mathbf{x}_{1}\otimes(\sqrt{2}\mathbf{y}_{3})\otimes\mathbf{z}_{2}+\pi\mathbf{x}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{y}_{3}\otimes\mathbf{z}_{5}=\mathbf{x}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{y}_{3}\otimes(\sqrt{2}\mathbf{z}_{2}+\pi\mathbf{z}_{5})
.

Example of formal addition:

3\mathbf{x}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{y}_{4}\otimes\mathbf{z}_{1}+5\mathbf{v}_{8}\otimes\mathbf{w}_{3}
can never be simplified further.

Rule 2:
For each given shape
[I_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]=[I_{1}]\times[I_{2}]\times\dots\times[I_{O}]
, choose a basis for
\mathbb{R}^{I_{o}}
for every
{o\in[O]}
.

This leads to
O
basises,
\mathscr{B}_{1}=\{\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{I_{1}}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{I_{1}},\dots,\mathscr{B}_{O}=\{\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{898471}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{898471}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{786091}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{786090}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{898471}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{898471}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{786091}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{786090}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{I_{O}}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{I_{O}}
.

Example:
For the given shape
[I_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]=[3]\times[2]
, one must choose a basis
\mathscr{B}_{1}
for
\mathbb{R}^{3}
and a basis
\mathscr{B}_{2}
for
\mathbb{R}^{2}
. For example, one might choose
\mathscr{B}_{1}=\{\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(3)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(3)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(3)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(3)\mathstrut$}}}}}},\mathbf{e}_{2}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(3)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(3)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(3)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(3)\mathstrut$}}}}}},\mathbf{e}_{3}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle({3})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle({3})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle({3})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle({3})\mathstrut$}}}}}}\}
and

Rule 3:
Every tensor of a given shape
[I_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]
must be written as a sum of elementary (i.e. rank-one) tensors such that each factor belongs to the corresponding basis chosen in the step above.

It is always possible to write a tensor this way, and to do so uniquely, since given basises

{\mathscr{B}_{1}=\{\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{I_{1}}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{I_{1}}}
,
\dots,\mathscr{B}_{O}=\{\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{898471}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{898471}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{786091}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{786090}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{898471}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{898471}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{786091}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{786090}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{I_{O}}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{I_{O}}
, the set:

\mathscr{B}\overset{\text{def}}{=}\{\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{i_{1}}\otimes\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{i_{2}}\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{898471}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{898471}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{786091}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{786090}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(O)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{i_{O}}:\mathbf{x}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(1)\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{i_{1}}\in\mathscr{B}_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\ In particular, when rule 4 is observed, the same variables are used for every mode of cubical tensors, which makes them easier to work with as non-commutative polynomials.

Example:
Consider when
[I_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{553683}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36572pt}{\resizebox{481937}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.36574pt}{\resizebox{481932}{268516}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]=[2]\times[2]\times[2]

4

Rule 5 (Optional):
Only consider cubical tensors, and of those only cubical tensors whose modes all have the same dimension, regardless of their order.

Example:
If one restricts to tensors of shape
[2]
,
[2]\times[2]
,
[2]\times[2]\times[2]
,
[2]\times[2]\times[2]\times[2]
,
\dots
, and always uses the same basis for
\mathbb{R}^{2}
, then regardless of the order of the tensor, the number of non-commuting variables is always
2
. Thus these tensors correspond to bivariate non-commutative polynomials in a very straightforward way
128
128

128

Strictly speaking one also needs to take care to include formal sums with “tensors or order zero”, i.e. scalars or constants, in order to be fully analogous with (commutative) polynomials.
. Similarly, tensors of shape
[3],[3]\times[3],[3]\times[3]\times[3]
,
[3]\times[3]\times[3]\times[3]
,
\dots
can be made to correspond to trivariate non-commutative polynomials.

To go from the result of applying rule 5 to something isomorphic to regular, commutative polynomials, one needs to do at least both of the following:

•

Restrict the subset of cubical tensors under consideration to only those which are symmetric,

•

Use a different product which preserves the symmetric property, i.e. a property under which symmetric tensors are closed.

This is because the regular tensor product does
not
preserve the property of being a symmetric tensor, i.e. given two symmetric tensors, the value of their tensor product need not be symmetric.

Example:
Letting as always
\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(2)\mathstrut$}}}}}},\mathbf{e}_{2}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle({2})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{732950}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle({2})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle({2})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{640458}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle({2})\mathstrut$}}}}}}

Appendix A.13
Separable Kronecker Covariance Structure

Having a separable Kronecker covariance structure means that the covariance matrix of the vectorized
130
130

130

The paper
[
190
]
uses the same unfolding conventions as
[
168
]
, which strongly suggests that the vectorization here is the colexicographical one. However, the type of vectorization used is never specified explicitly.
error tensors can be written as a sequence of Kronecker product factors:

\begin{array}[]{rcl}\bm{\Sigma}_{O}\otimes_{\operatorname{Kr}}\bm{\Sigma}_{O-1}\otimes_{\operatorname{Kr}}\cdots\otimes_{\operatorname{Kr}}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}&=&\operatorname{Cov}(\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i}))\\
&=&\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[(\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i})-\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i})])\otimes(\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i})-\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i})])\right]\\
&=&\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}])\otimes\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}])]\,.\end{array}

The last equation follows from the linearity of the colexicographical vectorization function.

Represent each covariance matrix
\bm{\Sigma}_{o}
in terms of its eigenvalue decomposition:

{\mathcal{S}\otimes\mathcal{S}:\mathbfcal{T}_{1}\otimes\mathbfcal{T}_{2}\mapsto\mathcal{S}(\mathbfcal{T}_{1})\otimes\mathcal{S}(\mathbfcal{T}_{2})}
, is also a linear function. The terms in the above summation are all of the form
{\mathcal{S}(\mathbfcal{I}_{m_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294060}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294061}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}})\otimes\mathcal{S}(\mathbfcal{I}_{m_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294060}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294061}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}})}=(\mathcal{S}\otimes\mathcal{S})(\mathbfcal{I}_{m_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294060}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294061}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}}\otimes\mathbfcal{I}_{m_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294060}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294061}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}})
. Therefore the right hand side of the above equation also equals:

(\mathcal{S}\otimes\mathcal{S})\left(\sum_{m_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}\in[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}\mathbfcal{I}_{m_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294060}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294061}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}}\otimes\mathbfcal{I}_{m_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294060}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294061}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}}\right)\,.

Note that the tensor
\sum_{m_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}\in[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}\mathbfcal{I}_{m_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294060}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294061}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}}\otimes\mathbfcal{I}_{m_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{412396}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294060}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-0.83333pt}{\resizebox{294061}{163840}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}}
corresponds
exactly
to the covariance tensor of a random tensor
\mathbfcal{U}_{i}
whose entries are all uncorrelated and which all have unit variance.

Thus the covariance tensor of
\mathbfcal{E}_{i}
is the same as the covariance tensor of the tensor:

\mathbfcal{U}_{i}\bullet_{1}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2}\cdots\bullet_{O}\bm{\Sigma}_{O}^{1/2}=\mathcal{S}(\mathbfcal{U}_{i})\,,

where again
\mathbfcal{U}_{i}
is
any
random tensor whose entries are uncorrelated and have unit variance. The above calculations should be compared with section 2.2 of
[
140
]
, noting that
k,K
in
[
140
]
correspond to
o,O
here, and in particular that the
\mathbf{A}_{k}
of
[
140
]
essentially correspond to the
\bm{\Sigma}_{o}^{1/2}
here so that the notation
\mathbf{Z}\times\mathbf{A}
corresponds to
\mathcal{S}(\mathbfcal{U}_{i})
. The definition of covariance tensor of the random tensor
\mathbfcal{E}_{i}
(corresponding to
\mathbf{Y}
of
[
140
]
) in
[
140
]
is a permutation of the modes of
\mathbb{E}[(\mathbfcal{E}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}])\otimes(\mathbfcal{E}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}])]
, i.e. essentially
\mathbb{E}[(\mathbfcal{E}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}])\otimes_{Z}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}])]
with
\otimes_{Z}
denoting a Zehfuss product for the only possible contiguous partition of the modes of
{\mathbfcal{E}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}]}
into
O
blocks, see appendix
A.9
.

The definition of covariance tensor from
[
140
]
is also such that the following is true:

\begin{array}[]{rcl}\mathbb{E}[(\mathbfcal{E}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}])\otimes_{Z}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}])]&=&\displaystyle\sum_{m_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}\in[M_{\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\displaystyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{607147}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.25pt}{$\textstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432927}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.875pt}{$\scriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.22687pt}{\resizebox{432929}{241212}{\hbox{\raisebox{0.625pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle[O]\mathstrut$}}}}}}]}(\mathbf{v}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1166868}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1166868}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{1060086}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.29443pt}{\resizebox{1152147}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.05pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{v}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1166868}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1166868}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{1060086}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.29443pt}{\resizebox{1152147}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.05pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{1})\otimes\cdots\otimes(\mathbf{v}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1268812}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1268812}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{1164108}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.59186pt}{\resizebox{1297778}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.18611pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{O}\otimes\mathbf{v}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1268812}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1268812}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{1164108}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.59186pt}{\resizebox{1297778}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.18611pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{O})\\
&=&\displaystyle\left(\sum_{m_{1}=1}^{{M_{1}}}\mathbf{v}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1166868}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1166868}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{1060086}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.29443pt}{\resizebox{1152147}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.05pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{v}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1166868}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1166868}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{1060086}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.29443pt}{\resizebox{1152147}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.05pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(m_{1})\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{1}\right)\otimes\cdots\otimes\left(\sum_{m_{O}=1}^{{M_{O}}}\mathbf{v}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1268812}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1268812}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{1164108}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.59186pt}{\resizebox{1297778}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.18611pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{O}\otimes\mathbf{v}^{\scriptsize\mathchoice{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1268812}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\displaystyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91203pt}{\resizebox{1268812}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.75pt}{$\textstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-1.91202pt}{\resizebox{1164108}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.22499pt}{$\scriptstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}{\raisebox{-2.59186pt}{\resizebox{1297778}{375921}{\hbox{\raisebox{1.18611pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle(m_{O})\mathstrut$}}}}}}_{O}\right)\\
&=&\bm{\Sigma}_{1}\otimes\bm{\Sigma}_{2}\otimes\cdots\otimes\bm{\Sigma}_{O}\,.\end{array}

Thus the intuition is that, for a separable Kronecker covariance structure,
\bm{\Sigma}_{1}
is the “covariance matrix for the first mode”,
\bm{\Sigma}_{2}
is the “covariance matrix for the second mode”, and so on.

In the case that all of the
\bm{\Sigma}_{o}
’s are positive definite, or equivalently in the case that all of the
\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}
’s are invertible, one can also say that the random tensor with the following definition:

\mathbfcal{U}_{i}\overset{\text{def}}{=}\mathbfcal{E}_{i}\bullet_{1}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\cdots\bullet_{O}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1/2}=\mathcal{S}^{-1}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i})

has all of its entries uncorrelated from one another and with unit variance.

When the residuals
\mathbfcal{E}_{i}
have what is called a multilinear normal distribution
[
225
]
, one can go further in making statements about the distribution of
\mathbfcal{E}_{i}
based on its covariance tensor alone. More specifically, as is partially explained in
[
225
]
, under such an assumption one can decompose the vectorized form of the tensor,
\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i})
, via the following relationship:

\begin{array}[]{rcl}\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}])&=&\\
\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{E}_{i})-\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}])&=&\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{U}_{i})\\
&=&(\bm{\Sigma}_{O}^{1/2}\otimes_{\operatorname{Kr}}\bm{\Sigma}_{O-1}^{1/2}\otimes_{\operatorname{Kr}}\cdots\otimes_{\operatorname{Kr}}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2})\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{U}_{i})\\
&=&\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}(\mathbfcal{U}_{i}\bullet_{1}\bm{\Sigma}_{1}^{1/2}\cdots\bullet_{O}\bm{\Sigma}_{O}^{1/2})\,,\end{array}

where by definition
\mathbfcal{U}_{i}
is a tensor whose entries consist of independent and identically distributed
{\mathscr{N}(0,1)}
random variables, and where the identity
[
126
]
[
166
]
from
6.5.1
giving the colexicographically vectorized form of the Tucker decomposition was used. Since
\operatorname{vec}_{\operatorname{col}}
is an invertible and linear function, the above relationship means that assuming the residuals have a multilinear normal distribution is equivalent to implicitly defining them in terms of a Tucker decomposition:

\mathbfcal{E}_{i}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbfcal{E}_{i}]+\mathbfcal{U}_{i}\bullet_{1}\bm{\Sigma}^{1/2}_{1}\cdots\bullet_{O}\bm{\Sigma}_{O}^{1/2}\,.

Note in particular that a commonly assumed case, where the entries of
\mathbfcal{E}_{i}
are all i.i.d. standard normal random variables, is (a rather uninteresting) special case of the above. The above gives a sense in which the statement that the matrix
\bm{\Sigma}_{o}
is “the covariance matrix for the
o
-th mode of
\mathbfcal{E}_{i}
” can be made precise for a multilinear normal distribution.

Appendix A.14
Relationships Between Eigen- and Singular Vectors and Values of Tensors

For a general non-cubical tensor, only singular values and singular vectors exist, so there is no need to wonder about their possible relationships with eigenpairs. However, starting already with arbitrary cubical tensors, one might begin to wonder whether certain relationships are guaranteed to exist. For example, the definition of eigenpair seems similar to the definition of singular value and vector tuple, and so one might wonder whether, given any eigenvector of a cubical tensor, the corresponding tuple of
O
copies of that eigenvector is also a singular vector tuple. However, one needs to keep in mind that the condition of being a mode-
o
eigenvector for some
o\in[O]
for a general cubical tensor corresponds to nothing stronger than satisfying at least one of the
O
necessary conditions for the corresponding tuple of
O
copies of that vector to be a singular vector tuple, much weaker than satisfying all of them simultaneously with the same value of
\lambda
or
\sigma
. In order to have its
O
copies be a singular vector tuple, the given vector would need to not only be a mode-
o
eigenvector simultaneously for all
O
modes of the tensor, it would also need to correspond to the same eigenvalue for each mode. Since, as discussed previously, higher-order tensors need not have the same eigenvalues for all modes, those tensors for which this is the case cannot have any singular vector tuples consisting of
O
copies (up to signs) of the same vector, and thus their eigenpairs and singular values and singular vector tuples will be unrelated.

Even when the various modes of a cubical tensor happen to have the same eigenvalues (e.g. as in the matrix case), they need not necessarily have the same eigenvectors, and even in this case any eigenvector which does not correspond to all modes of the tensor has no chance of corresponding to a singular vector tuple of
O
copies (up to signs) of itself. It seems a direct consequence from the definitions that a vector has
O
copies of itself (up to signs) as a singular vector tuple if and only if it is an eigenvector simultaneously for all modes corresponding to the same eigenvalue. In particular a tensor has a singular vector tuple consisting of
O
copies (up to signs) of the same vector if and only if it has such an eigenvector. Thus the definitions of eigenpair and singular value and vector tuple for a cubical tensor are not as similar as lazily glancing would suggest. One might still wonder whether the remaining singular vector tuples with at least two distinct (up to signs) vectors have any weaker relationships with the eigenvectors for any of the modes, but already the case of matrices suggests that this is not the case. However, when the cubical tensor is symmetric,
every
eigenvector automatically satisfies all of the
O
necessary conditions with the same
\lambda
. So one can conclude that that every eigenpair of a
symmetric
tensor corresponds (up to signs) to a singular value and a singular vector tuple consisting of
O
copies (up to signs) of the same vector. This leads to the questions of whether all singular values and singular vector tuples of a higher-order symmetric tensor can be so characterized, and if not, what can be said about those singular vector tuples of a higher-order symmetric tensor consisting of distinct (even up to signs) vectors.

Like the case of order-two tensors (matrices), the largest
\ell^{2}
-singular value of a symmetric higher-order tensor equals the absolute value of its largest-in-magnitude
\ell^{2}
-eigenvalue, and (up to signs) the corresponding tuple of
\ell^{2}
-singular vectors is the same as the corresponding
\ell^{2}
-eigenvector
[
136
]
. For symmetric matrices, the analogous statements are also true for the smaller singular values and smaller-in-magnitude eigenvalues. It is not immediately obvious whether this is also true for higher-order tensors. This is because the variational problem defining
\ell^{2}
-singular values for arbitrary tensors (not necessarily symmetric) is related to the optimization problem defining the best rank-one approximation in such a way that, if
\mathbf{v}_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathbf{v}_{O}
is the best rank-one approximation, then the largest
\ell^{2}
-singular value
\sigma_{1}=\prod_{o=1}^{O}||\mathbf{v}_{o}||_{2}
and for each of the corresponding
\ell^{2}
-singular vectors
\mathbf{x}_{o}=\mathbf{v}_{o}/||\mathbf{v}_{o}||_{2}
[
136
]
[
192
]
. (In fact this relationship allows one to prove the NP-hardness of finding a best rank-one approximation starting from the fact that finding the largest
\ell^{2}
-singular value is NP-hard
[
136
]
. Moreover just like for matrices the largest
\ell^{2}
-singular value equals, basically by definition, the spectral norm of the tensor, a fact utilized in
[
297
]
.) In the case that the tensor is symmetric, a theorem by Banach guarantees that the corresponding optimization problem for the largest-in-magnitude
\ell^{2}
-eigenvalue coincides with the problem for finding the largest
\ell^{2}
-singular value (cf. the statement about best rank-one Waring decompositions made in section
9.6
).

One might therefore suppose that the analogous statements for smaller
\ell^{2}
-singular values and smaller-in-magnitude
\ell^{2}
-eigenvalues are not true for higher-order tensors. The method of proof used for the largest
\ell^{2}
-singular value and largest-in-magnitude
\ell^{2}
-eigenvalue seems to break down since, for higher-order tensors, best rank-
r
and rank-
(r+1)
approximations need not exist, and even if they do exist they are generally unrelated to each other, unlike the matrix case. For the matrix case, one would use the fact that, given a matrix
\mathbf{T}
and its best rank-one approximation
\mathbf{T}_{(1)}
, its best rank-two approximation would be
\mathbf{T}_{(1)}+\mathbf{T}_{(2)}
, where
\mathbf{T}_{(2)}
denotes the best rank one approximation of
\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{T}_{(1)}
. For a given higher order tensor
\mathbfcal{T}
, even though a best rank-one approximation
\mathbfcal{T}_{(1)}
to
\mathbfcal{T}
and a best rank-one approximation
\mathbfcal{T}_{(2)}
to
\mathbfcal{T}-\mathbfcal{T}_{(1)}
will exist, in general
\mathbfcal{T}_{(1)}+\mathbfcal{T}_{(2)}
is not the best rank-two approximation to
\mathbfcal{T}
and in fact such an approximation need not even exist. On the other hand, even though
\mathbfcal{T}_{(1)}+\mathbfcal{T}_{(2)}
is not the best rank-two approximation to
\mathbfcal{T}
, one might still hope that
||\mathbfcal{T}_{(2)}||_{F}
is the second largest
\ell^{2}
-singular value and that the corresponding
\ell^{2}
-singular vector tuple is the same as the tensor product factors in
\mathbfcal{T}_{(2)}
up to scaling. As mentioned before, in the case that
\mathbfcal{T}
is symmetric, a theorem from Banach guarantees that
\mathbfcal{T}_{(1)}
will be symmetric, and thus that also
\mathbfcal{T}-\mathbfcal{T}_{(1)}
will be symmetric, which in turn by the theorem implies that
\mathbfcal{T}_{(2)}
will be symmetric, and so one might hope in that case that
||\mathbfcal{T}_{(2)}||_{F}
is also the absolute value of the second largest-in-magnitude
\ell^{2}
-eigenvalue of
\mathbfcal{T}
and that the single repeated tensor product factor defining
\mathbfcal{T}_{(2)}
will be (up to scaling and signs) the corresponding
\ell^{2}
-eigenvector.

However, if none of this is true, then one might also suppose that the
\ell^{2}
-singular vector tuple corresponding to the second largest
\ell^{2}
-singular value of a higher-order symmetric tensor could possibly (even up to signs) consist of distinct vectors, rather than
O
copies of a related
\ell^{2}
-eigenvector. Even though it is fairly clear that the eigenpairs of a higher-order symmetric tensor have to correspond to singular tuples with
O
copies (up to signs) of the eigenvector and the eigenvalue the same (up to signs) as the singular value, the converse relationship is much less clear except in the case of the
\ell^{2}
definitions for the largest
\ell^{2}
-singular value only. It is less straightforward to discern whether every singular vector tuple of a higher-order symmetric tensor must consist of
O
copies of the same (up to signs) vector (recall that when a singular vector tuple does, the repeated vector is automatically an eigenvector and the singular value is up to signs automatically an eigenvalue).

spaces
are
restricted
to
be
linear
functions
in

of

\mathsf{Vect}_{\mathbb{R}}
,
whereas

of

\mathsf{Set}

all

between
any

are
also
present.
So
while
the

{f:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}}

given

(x,y)\mapsto(x^{2},y^{2})

is
in

\mathsf{Mor}_{\mathsf{Set}}(\mathbb{R}^{2},\mathbb{R}^{2})
,
it
is

not

in

\mathsf{Mor}_{\mathsf{Vect}_{\mathbb{R}}}(\mathbb{R}^{2},\mathbb{R}^{2})

since
it
is
not
a
linear
function.

f.

Recall

(\mathbb{V}_{1},\dots,\mathbb{V}_{D})

\bigotimes_{\mathbb{T}_{2}}\overset{\text{def}}{=}\Upsilon^{-1}\circ\bigotimes_{\mathbb{T}_{1}}
.
Cf.

f.

Actually
the
notion
of
“free
vector
space”
opens
its
own
separate
can
of
worms,
since
it
is
also
defined
via
a
universal
property
which
only

a
vector
space
up

and
does
not

to
any
particular
construction
over
another.
The
approach
taken
in
section
3.1.2
of

[
129
]

for

free

is
very
similar
to
the
usual

of
